text.head: I. INTRODUCTION
text.p:
High-Frequency Inductive Power Transfer (HF-IPT) ex-
ploits the fact that large diameter, high quality factor (Q) MHz
air-core inductors can be realized and used in the magnetic
link, allowing much lighter systems to be created than by using
kHz, ferrite-enhanced counterparts [1]. A large diameter coil
with high Q can enable meaningful power transfer distance
with high link efficiency [2], [3]. This coil can then be
combined with Class E-type circuit topologies that are tolerant
to load variations (e.g. Class EF topologies) to make a practical
system [4]-[9].

The efficiency of HF-IPT coil drivers has been improving,
partly through the use of wide bandgap technology, such as
GaN and Silicon Carbide (SiC) [10], [11] and partly through
detailed modeling and optimisation [12]. Now, the dominant
sources of losses are the inductors (other than the primary coil)
present in the coil drivers.

In several Class EF inverter designs (for example, see
Fig. 1), the lossiest inductor is the ϕ-branch inductor (L ϕ ).

text.p:
The addition of the ϕ-branch enhances the range of design
capabilities compared to the traditional Class E inverter [13] by
providing two extra degrees of freedom. This enables higher
power capability of the inverter with lower device stresses,
more effective absorption of the device non-linear output
capacitance, and load-independence with a finite choke [4],
[12]. However, this comes with the cost of the current in the
ϕ-branch inductor (L ϕ ) often being close in magnitude to that
of the primary coil (L s1 ). Because of this, the losses in the
ϕ-branch inductor can be significant if its Q is not sufficiently
large. Indeed, air-core ϕ-branch inductors have been shown to
consume around 20 % of the total losses [12].

Moreover, the ϕ-branch current can contain substantial har-
monic components up to the third order. These harmonics can
play a significant role in how this inductor should be ideally
optimised. A bespoke inductor solution, which accounts for
these higher order harmonics, would add a degree of freedom
in the optimisation process, making it easier to minimise the
losses in the ϕ-branch.

Additionally, for practicality, the ϕ-branch inductor must be
much smaller than the transmit and receive coils in the HF-IPT
system. Recent work has shown that small, low-loss inductors
may be achieved for frequencies in the tens of MHz by using
cored designs [14]. This suggests that cored components can
be used in HF-IPT systems without sacrificing the overall
light-weight benefits of MHz operation.

In this work, we designed and built a low-loss cored
inductor for the ϕ-branch of a 13.56 MHz, 70 W Class EF 2
inverter [12] (Fig. 1). This inductor achieves low loss by using
a modified pot core (MP) structure that is well-suited for the

an experimental comparison with five different inductors, in-

EF 2 inverter. The MP inductor significantly outperformed the
other inductors, achieving less than half the power loss, which
resulted in a 0.4 % increase in system efficiency over the best
comparison inductor, corresponding to a 6 % reduction in total
system loss.

In this paper, we detail the streamlined design process
used to achieve such a low-loss inductor for multi-frequency
MHz applications with the MP structure. We then discuss
the design of the comparison inductors. Finally, we present
the experimental setup as well as the component and system
performance of all five tested inductors.
text.head:
II. A ϕ-BRANCH INDUCTOR DESIGN USING A MODIFIED
POT CORE STRUCTURE
text.p:
For the example 13.56 MHz Class EF 2 inverter, the ϕ-
branch current has a main frequency of operation at the second
harmonic. This current, shown in Fig. 2, also has substantial
fundamental and third harmonic components. Therefore, to
achieve a low-loss ϕ-branch inductor, we need a design that
is optimised for this multi-frequency current.

A low-loss cored inductor design that is suitable for this
HF-IPT application is the modular modified pot core (MP)
structure introduced in [15], [16]. The MP structure looks
similar to a standard pot core geometry but has a larger
core area to window area ratio as well as many small gaps
distributed vertically throughout its core (Fig. 3).

In general, MP core geometries are constructed from a
modular set of core pieces that form a core set. Each core set
is defined by its footprint diameter, which serves as a base for
the set. Using a single core set, different MP core geometries
can easily be constructed by stacking different numbers of
core pieces on top of this footprint base. This modularity
provides flexibility for designing inductors tailored to specific
applications.

To evaluate the performance of the MP structure for this
application, we designed and built a ϕ-branch inductor using
this structure. To simplify the design process, we leveraged
an existing MP core geometry developed in [16] and used
solid round wire. 1 The target inductance for this inductor was
250 nH. Full specifications of the final MP inductor design are
listed in Table I.

In this section, we provide an overview of how the MP
structure achieves low loss. Afterwards, we walk through the
process for designing and building the ϕ-branch inductor using
the MP structure. This design process is suitable for quickly
generating low-loss inductor designs and can be used in any
application with high-frequency ac currents.
text.head: A. Low-Loss Features of the MP Structure:
text.p:
The MP struc-
ture's core geometry is specifically designed to achieve low
core and winding loss for large, high-frequency ac currents.

To achieve low core loss, which scales with the B fields in
the core, the MP structure includes two main features to keep
the B fields low. First, the MP structure has a larger core
to window area ratio than conventional cores. For inductor
designs intended for large ac currents, having a large window
area for the winding is not crucial for low winding loss since
current mainly flows within a skin depth of the conductor and
not through the entire cross-section. However, having a large
cross-sectional core area is crucial for low core loss since it
can greatly reduce the core's flux density B. Therefore, the
MP structure dedicates more of its volume to the core to take
advantage of this low-penalty trade-off.

Second, to help achieve low core loss, the MP structure
has many small gaps distributed vertically throughout its core,
which form a quasi-distributed gap [17]. These gaps add
reluctance to the core's magnetic flux path, which reduces the
B fields, and thus loss, in the core.

To achieve low winding loss, the MP structure uses a closed-
core geometry designed to shape the magnetic fields around
the winding. This field shaping enables current to more evenly
distribute in the conductor, reducing the winding's effective
resistance. In the MP structure, the winding is also limited
to a single layer to reduce losses due to the proximity effect
between multiple layers of conductors.

Additionally, the quasi-distributed gap in the MP structure
helps to achieve low winding loss. In typical designs with a
single lumped gap, magnetic fields at the gap fringe outwards
into the window area. In conductors near the gap, current then
crowds towards these fringing fields instead of distributing in
the available conduction area, which increases winding loss.
With a quasi-distributed gap, however, the gap is distributed
along the core, thus reducing the magnitude of fringing fields
at each smaller gap while also distributing their location. By
doing so, this type of gap reduces the impact of fringing fields
on winding loss.
text.head: B. Design Process for the MP Inductor:
text.p:
To design the ϕ-
branch inductor using the MP structure, we used a streamlined
design process that prioritized ease of design over exact opti-
misation. 2 To do this, we only considered MP core geometries
that were previously developed in [16]. After selecting a
geometry, we used hand calculations to roughly optimise the
MP design and then quickly fine-tuned it in 2D Finite Element
Analysis (FEA) simulations. This method of rough estimation
can still yield low-loss designs since the optimisation curve
for the MP structure is relatively flat near its minimum loss
point [15]. Below, we detail the design process for the ϕ-
branch MP inductor, which is also summarised in Fig. 4.

First, we chose a target volume for the inductor at around
4.0 cm 3 , which is similar to the volume of the ϕ-branch induc-
tor used in [12]. Then, we looked for a MP core geometry in
this size. To do this, we looked at existing MP core sets listed
in [16]'s Table I to find an appropriate core set to use. Since
the target volume is relatively small, we selected the smallest
existing core set, MP17, which has a footprint diameter of
17 mm. To meet our target volume, we then calculated the
required height of stacked core pieces for the design, which
was 14 mm. The resulting MP core geometry had a height-to-
diameter ratio of 0.8 and is denoted as MP17-0.8, per [16].

text.p:
Next, we looked for a core material with low loss in our
frequency range of interest from 13.56 MHz to 40.68 MHz.
For this reason, we chose Fair-Rite 67 [18].

Using the MP17 core set, we optimised the MP inductor
design for minimum loss by adjusting the number of turns and
total gap reluctance (which is later used to derive the required
total gap length).

To do this, we first modeled core loss as a function of the
number of turns using the iGSE core loss model [19], [20].
This model uses an improved version of the original Steinmetz
equation [21], called iGSE, that can handle multi-frequency
waveforms, making it suitable for modeling core loss in the
example ϕ-branch inductor design.

For this design, we simplified core loss calculations for the
MP17-0.8 core geometry by modeling it with three lumped
effective geometric parameters that represent an equivalent
toroid with uniformly distributed B fields. The parameters
were: the effective core cross-sectional area A e , the effective
core length l e , and the effective core volume V e . To estimate
A e , we leveraged the fact that the MP core geometry was de-
signed to have similar effective cross-sectional area throughout
most of the core [15]. So, for simplicity, we calculated A e as
the cross-sectional area of the center core section, known as
the center post, for A e = 104 mm 2 . To estimate l e , we looked
at the flux path through the core, which encircles the window.
Since the path includes gaps, we estimated l e as less than the
full path length, estimating it as twice the window height for
l e = 15.1 mm. Finally, to estimate V e , we took the product of
A e and l e for V e = 1.6 cm 3 .

To model core loss, the iGSE method takes a complex
current waveform and divides it into simpler single-frequency
sub-waveforms or 'loops'. Doing so helps with modeling core
loss more accurately since core loss parameters are often
provided under single-frequency conditions. So, for the multi-
frequency ϕ-branch current, we divided it into two loops,
one with a local frequency of 24 MHz and the other with a
frequency at 32 MHz (see Fig. 2).

to calculate the B field waveforms in the core as a function
of the number of turns N :

Finally, using our core and winding loss models, we swept
over different MP designs to find the one with minimum
loss. The resulting optimal MP17-0.8 inductor design had 3
turns with an estimated core loss of 140 mW and an estimated
copper loss of 490 mW for a total loss of 630 mW.

From there, we finalised the design of the MP inductor's
quasi-distributed gaps through an iterative process using 2D
FEA simulations. The MP structure has quasi-distributed gaps
in two sections of the core, the center post and the outer
section. These gaps are composed of alternating core pieces
and gaps, with core pieces on both ends of the stack. So for
N gap gaps in a stack, there are N gap + 1 core pieces. The
quasi-distributed gaps are defined by the total gap length and
the number of stacked core pieces and gaps in each section.
For design simplicity, we constrained the MP design to have
the same number of core pieces and gaps in both sections, as
well as the same core piece height (defined by the MP core
set) and total gap length.

To design the quasi-distributed gaps, we first developed an
initial simulation design. To do this, we roughly estimated the
total gap length l gap needed to achieve the target inductance
by using a reluctance model of the inductor. This model is
intended to quickly generate an initial design to iterate on and
isn't intended to provide an extremely accurate gap length.

In this model, inductance L is defined by the core and
gap reluctances R as well as the number of turns N using
L = N 2 /(R core + R gap ). To simplify calculations, we es-
timated the reluctances using the MP core's effective geo-
metric parameters (l e , A e ) and the core material's relative
permeability µ r while neglecting fringing fields from the gaps:
R core ≈ l e /(µ r µ 0 A e ) and R gap ≈ l gap /(µ 0 A e ), where µ 0 is
the permeability of free space. Using these equations, the total

Using this estimated gap length, we picked the number of
core pieces (and gaps) that would bring the MP design close
to its target height of 14 mm. Then, we simulated this initial
design and checked its simulated inductance. on the
simulated inductance, we adjusted the total gap length and
number of core pieces/gaps to better meet the target inductance
and continued to make these iterative adjustments until we had
a design that met the target inductance near the target volume.

After finalising the design, we built the MP inductor (Fig. 5)
using the construction process detailed in [15]. For this
prototyping process, the inductor was constructed in sections
by alternately stacking core pieces and plastic spacers to form
the quasi-distributed gaps. The sections were then assembled
together. Custom 3D-printed jigs were used to help with
stacking the cores as well as with constructing the winding.
text.head: III. INDUCTOR DESIGNS USING OFF-THE-SHELF PARTS
text.p:
For comparison, we investigated and built four other ϕ-
branch inductor designs for the example 13.56 MHz Class EF 2
inverter using off-the-shelf parts:

The inductors were all designed for a target inductance of
250 nH and for a similar volume range as the MP inductor
design (constrained by part availability). Each inductor was
optimised for the ϕ-branch current (Fig. 2) in the example
Class EF 2 inverter using conventional design approaches. All
designs also used solid round wire, as was done with the
MP inductor design. The physical characteristics for the four
designs are listed in Table II, with photos shown in Fig. 5.

The following subsections discuss the rationale and design
process for each inductor design:

text.head: A. Ferrite Toroid Design:
text.p:
To demonstrate the importance
of having a gap in a ferrite core to keep core loss low, we
designed an ungapped ferrite toroid inductor for comparison.
Because this design is not gapped, the core is expected to have
large B fields and hence large core loss. This inductor design
used a toroid with a similar volume to the MP inductor and
the same core material: Fair-Rite 5967000601 (67) [18]. The
number of turns was chosen to achieve the target inductance
of 250 nH.
text.head: B. Iron Powder Toroid Designs:
text.p:
An alternative approach to
using ferrite in cores (ideally with a gap) is to use powder
core materials. These materials usually have worse core loss
characteristics in the MHz range than low-loss ferrite mate-
rials. However, they generally have very low permeabilities
and thus act as a perfectly distributed gap core, which helps
to achieve lower core B fields for lower core loss. The
core's distributed gap also reduces the effect of fringing fields
incurring additional loss in the winding.

For our example comparison, we designed two inductor
designs, each using a different iron powder core material with
relatively low core loss: Micrometals material mix no. -2 and
no. -6. For both designs, we selected a core size with a similar
volume to the MP inductor (T80) and used the following
cores: Micrometals T80-2 (M2) [24] and Micrometals T80-
6 (M6) [25]. The number of turns in each design was chosen
to achieve the target inductance of 250 nH.
text.head: C. Air-Core Design:
text.p:
In addition to the above cored inductor
designs, we tested a comparable air-core design. To do this,
we bought an off-the-shelf air-core inductor near the target
inductance of 250 nH: Coilcraft 2014VS-251MED (VS) [26],
which is nominally 257 nH.

Per Table II, the air-core inductor's physical box volume
is smaller than the MP inductor; however, its effective box
volume is larger. Without a magnetic core, the air-core inductor
has significant fringing fields that are sensitive to nearby metal
objects. To prevent interactions with these fields, which can
substantially reduce the inductor's performance, extra space is
needed around the inductor. If, for example, each dimension
of the air-core inductor was padded with a very small 10%
buffer (excluding the -z direction), its effective box size would
be 14 mm x 22 mm x 16 mm for an effective box volume of
4.9 cm 3 , which is closer to that of the MP inductor.
text.head: IV. EXPERIMENTAL SETUP AND RESULTS
text.p:
To test the five high-frequency inductors (Table II), we
first measured their impedance using the Keysight E4990A
impedance analyser with a 42941A probe and a custom fixture.
The results are shown in Fig. 6. All the inductors have around
250 nH inductance, as designed. The inductances also stay
relatively constant past the third harmonic at 40.68 MHz,
suggesting that the inductors would behave as designed in the
example inverter.

Using these impedance measurements, we created a fitted
ac circuit diagram model of these inductors, shown in Fig. 7,
with parameter values given in Table III. In this model, R s is
related to conduction (wire) losses, C s sets the Self Resonance
Frequency (SRF) as well as the frequency dependence of the
Q factor, R p could be regarded as a rough measure of core
losses (at small-signal), and L is the intrinsic inductance.

Based on these results, the MP inductor has the highest
SRF, which is confirmed both by the flatness of the inductance
measurement in Fig. 6 and the lowest parasitic capacitance
value in Table III. Furthermore, the ac circuit parameters from
Table III suggest that the MP structure has lower core losses
compared to the ungapped toroid of the same core material
(67). Even though the two inductors have very similar R s due
to the same number of turns (Table II), the 67 toroid has almost
4 times lower R p .

Next, we took small-signal Q measurements of the five
inductors as an initial evaluation of their performance, shown
in Fig. 6. Based on these measurements, the MP inductor has
the highest Q at the second harmonic, which is the dominant
component of the ϕ-branch current, per the inverter simulation

After this initial evaluation, we tested the five inductors in
a Class EF 2 inverter coupled inductively to a resonant ac load

inverter's overall efficiency is sensitive to the performance of
the ϕ-branch inductor because it minimises transistor losses
through a combination of Zero Voltage Switching (ZVS),
Zero Voltage Derivative Switching (ZVDS), and high dc-to-ac
current gain. This feature enables us to get reliable data, even
when the differences in performance of the inductors under
test are marginal.

To reduce the sensitivity of the circuit to the unavoidable
inductance variations in Fig. 6, the total inductance of the
ϕ-branch was set at around 400 nH, higher than the indi-
vidual inductance of the inductor under test. The additional
inductance in every case was provided by adding an extra air-
core inductor [26]. With this setup, the tuning of the inverter
remained constant, and any performance differences can be
attributed only to the inductor under test.

To confirm identical circuit tuning for all instances, as well
as resonance at the second harmonic, we took impedance
measurements of the ϕ-branch for all the inductors (Fig. 8).
These measurements were taken with all the components
soldered on the Printed Circuit Board (PCB) to include layout
parasitics. The matching in tuning was also confirmed from
the experimental waveforms of the drain voltage, the ϕ-
branch current, and the voltage across the inductors in Fig. 9.
The voltage across the inductor was measured indirectly by
measuring the drain and ϕ-branch capacitor voltages and then
subtracting them. The reason for such an indirect measurement
is because at these frequencies, the capacitance of the probe
(several pF typically) in parallel with the inductor would
significantly affect its impedance and thus produce unreliable
data. For the voltage measurements, we used isolated optical
probes (Tektronix IsoVu) for the lowest possible capacitive

It must be noted that because of the additional wire loop
in the ϕ-branch for the attachment of the current clamp
(Keysight N2783B), the impedance of the ϕ-branch slightly
deviated from the ideal value, and thus we increased the
operating frequency to 13.65 MHz to maintain ZVDS, which
is insignificant for the inductor performance. Also, the output
power of the inverter was kept at 70 W in order to maintain the
ϕ-branch current within the limits of the current probe. The
slightly lower amplitude in harmonics of the measurements in
Table IV compared to the simulation in Fig. 2 could also partly
be attributed to the non-flat response of the current probe at
this frequency range.

(left). The MP has the best overall performance, followed by

Even though the VS and the M6 have lower permeability
than the ferrite used in MP, its unique structure successfully
enhances the core's performance at high frequencies. Figure 10
(right) displays the fraction of the total losses that is attributed
to the inductor, where the MP inductor has about half the
losses of the next best performing counterpart. These numbers
were extrapolated by combining the relative differences in
efficiency with the already known losses of the VS inductor
in this inverter design from previous work in [12]. Given all
the measurement uncertainties of this high frequency setup,
accurate measurements of the absolute loss of the inductors
are challenging, but the relative figures we provide are highly
reliable since the same unavoidable error sources are present
in all instances. The outcomes of Fig. 10 also agree with the
trend of the temperature measurements in Table V. Another
noteworthy result from Table V is that the transistors in all
cases have almost identical temperature, which confirms that
any differences in output power are primarily due to the
inductor performance.
text.head: V. CONCLUSION
text.p:
This paper provides a streamlined process for designing
low-loss inductors using the MP structure for complex high-
frequency magnetic applications with multi-frequency cur-
rents. It was experimentally demonstrated that the MP struc-
ture is an effective option for such applications, as it out-
performed every other comparison counterpart in an example
13.56 MHz, 70 W Class EF 2 inverter used for HF-IPT. The
MP inductor achieved half the loss of its counterparts and
improved system efficiency by 0.4 % compared to the best
comparison inductor, corresponding to a 6 % reduction in
total loss. This suggests that the streamlined design process
is effective in quickly achieving low-loss inductor designs.
